title: The ‘Super-Terrorist’ We Still Can’t Escape
gist: Reviewing Joby Warrick's biography of Carlos the Jackal, Juliette Kayyem argues today's threat landscape has reverted from bin Laden's mass-casualty model to Carlos's performative, for-hire model — with Russia and Iran now paying criminal networks for deniable attacks in the West, and lone actors courting infamy without coherent ideology.

insights.claim: Carlos's most durable legacy is the terrorist-for-hire brand, which continues today with states such as Russia and Iran paying criminal networks to attack political enemies in the West while retaining plausible deniability.
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: State-sponsored deniable violence via criminal proxies is the operative security risk in Europe — it blurs attribution, complicates sanctions responses and keeps corporate security spending elevated.
insights.quote: countries such as Russia and Iran paying criminal networks to do their global bidding by attacking political enemies in the West, getting what they want with plausible deniability
insights.locator: Carlos’s most lasting legacy was in treating violence

insights.claim: By 1979 Carlos had degenerated into a contractor for authoritarian clients — including Romania's Nicolae Ceausescu, who hired him to assassinate dissidents across Europe and bomb Radio Free Europe's Romanian studio in Munich.
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that state outsourcing of political violence to freelancers is a recurring, not novel, tool — useful when assessing current unattributed incidents in Europe.
insights.locator: By 1979, Carlos was reduced to a man for hire

insights.claim: State sponsors are unreliable partners for their own proxies: Qaddafi armed the OPEC attack then turned on Carlos when he sought refuge, and Carlos was ultimately betrayed by one of his own, Swiss militant Bruno Breguet, who served as a CIA informant.
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: Proxy relationships are inherently unstable, which is both a vulnerability for sponsors and an intelligence opportunity for Western agencies.

themes.theme: The casualty/attention framework has flipped twice

insights.claim: Brian Jenkins' classic formulation — terrorists want 'a lot of people watching, not a lot of people dead' — described the pre-1990s era, before the National Commission on Terrorism warned by 2000 that terrorists now wanted both a lot of people dead and a lot of people watching.
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: A two-axis model (casualties vs. attention) for classifying threat regimes; the current regime has reverted toward the attention axis, implying lower expected casualties but higher event frequency.
insights.quote: a lot of people watching, not a lot of people dead
insights.locator: When I first entered the counterterrorism world in 1997

insights.claim: Today's terror threat is more dispersed, random and ideologically incoherent than in bin Laden's era — 'plenty of executioners and no masterminds.'
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: Decapitation strategies targeting leadership no longer reduce the threat; detection must shift to individual behavioral signals, reshaping where security budgets go.
insights.quote: There are plenty of executioners and no masterminds.
insights.locator: Although Carlos failed at the one thing

insights.claim: Performative violence now generates its own celebrity: lone wolves write manifestos as if already famous, a healthcare executive's killer becomes a superstar, and the alleged shooters in multiple assassination attempts on Trump appeared to have no clear political allegiance.
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: Violence motivated by infamy rather than ideology is nearly impossible to profile by affiliation — a persistent tail risk for executives and public figures, and a driver of corporate protection spending.
insights.quote: Violence is performed for an audience, the spectacle, the symbolism.
insights.locator: But Carlos’s love of the limelight

insights.claim: Social media has made the filming and streaming of violence ubiquitous, giving performative terrorism an amplification channel that Carlos had to obtain through tabloid journalists.
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: Platform amplification is the modern force multiplier for attention-seeking violence — a continuing source of content-moderation regulatory pressure.
insights.locator: But Carlos’s love of the limelight also resonates today

themes.theme: Branding and the gap between reputation and capability

insights.claim: Carlos's fearsome reputation vastly exceeded his operational competence — he botched or aborted many missions, the Joseph Sieff assassination attempt failed, the 1975 Orly rocket attacks failed to destroy the El Al planes, and a friend judged him 'no mastermind... an executioner.'
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: Adversary reputation is a poor proxy for capability; the same skepticism should be applied to modern threat actors whose brand outruns their record.
insights.locator: As Carlos realized his growing isolation

insights.claim: The 'Jackal' name was pure branding — a tabloid applied it after Forsyth's novel was found at his London safehouse and Carlos adopted it because it worked, just as 'Carlos' was a cell recruiter's nickname.
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: Illustrates how media naming conventions manufacture the very mystique that drives policy overreaction — a caution for how today's threats get labeled.
insights.quote: Carlos adopted it as his own because it was good branding.
insights.locator: The name we know Sánchez by

insights.claim: Carlos's ideological commitment was hollow — he professed to hate Western excess while loving its hotels, cars and jewelry, converted to Islam only late, and the Palestinian cause became irrelevant to his actions once he turned mercenary.
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: Ideological framing can be a recruitment veneer over personal motive — counter-messaging aimed at ideology misses the actual driver.
insights.locator: His philosophy, if he had one at all

insights.claim: The 1975 OPEC raid in Vienna — Carlos's signature operation — killed three and resulted in around 60 hostages being flown to Algeria and Libya, and was launched precisely because he needed a win after prior failures.
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: Spectacular attacks can be driven by an actor's need to restore credibility after failure — a behavioral predictor of escalation following setbacks.
insights.quote: I am the famous Carlos! You know who I am
insights.locator: This is not the man the world witnessed decades ago

insights.claim: Carlos surveilled the wealthy bin Laden family as kidnapping targets in Lebanon's Chouf mountains in the mid-1970s before abandoning the plan for the OPEC attack, and his reign ended in Sudan — the same permissive environment that later sheltered bin Laden until his 1996 expulsion to Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Juliette Kayyem
insights.so_what: Permissive jurisdictions, not individual actors, are the durable enabling variable — a reason to watch ungoverned space rather than personalities.
insights.quote: To describe the country’s political climate as permissive for terrorists would be to understate the case
